newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA POSSESSES UNIQUE GLAMOUR.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA POSSESSES UNIQUE GLAMOUR.

text.p: No skier has quite the glamour of Alberto Tomba, a man whose off-piste escapades have brought him publicity on an unprecedented scale in the decade since he won his first race in Sestriere.
He has modelled boxer shorts, appeared naked on magazine covers, been linked to Hollywood and taken to court for karate-kicking photographers.
Internet admirers have bombarded the 30-year-old from Bologna with passionate messages.

Who else but Tomba could win a race and then roar delightedly, as he did in his youth: "I am an animal"? Or boast that he used to return home to bed after a night partying about the time other racers were getting up?

The unanswered question is whether the Italian's hour wil come round again at next week's world championships here or whether his time is up after almost retiring last year at the end of an exhausting season.
Tomba has crashed heavily in training, missed races because of influenza and is well behind on vital preparations.
Meanwhile new faces, such as the technically brilliant Austrian Thomas Sykora, are challenging his supremacy.

But Tomba, on the piste every bit as explosive as his nickname "La Bomba" suggests, is a skier impossible to write off, an athlete with a knack of pulling out his best just when it seems the pressure is unbearable.
That said, the omens do not look overly promising for the double world and triple Olympic champion.
On the plus side, the north-western Italian resort of Sestriere brought Tomba his first World Cup wins back-to-back triumphs in a slalom and a giant in November 1987.
For the sake of symmetry as much as anything else, Tomba is determined to repeat the triumph 10 years on.
But he may not want to recall his words before the 1996 Sierra Nevada championships, where he went on to win both giant and slalom titles, although they are worth repeating:
"I've always been lucky in even years," he declared of major tournaments. "Uneven years have always been unlucky."
The statistics bear him out. He won the Olympic slalom and giant titles in Albertville, or "Albertoville" as he dubbed it, in 1988 and the giant title in Lillehammer in 1992.

The world championships, held in odd years, brought him nothing more than a bronze in the giant at Crans-Montana in 1987 and a lack of snow forced the postponement of the 1995 championships which were then held in Spain in 1996.
In the 1989 and 1991 championships he finished fourth, seventh and sixth and in Morioka, Japan, in 1993 he failed to finish at all after being laid low by a stomach bug.
Tomba arrived in Sierra Nevada last year to local outrage after comparing the southern Spanish resort to Africa.

His concentration was also in some doubt after he had angrily lobbed a heavy glass trophy and champagne bottle at a press photographer who had sold nude photographs of the skier relaxing in a Swiss sauna to an Italian magazine.
He left with two gold medals in his luggage.
Since those glory days. the Alberto Tomba story has turned into a tale of incidents, injury and influenza.
He fell heavily in pre-season training in October and struggled back in time for Christmas with a remarkable second place in a slalom at Madonna di Campiglio in Italy.
But, entering the New Year, he again fell in a special three-run exhibition slalom on Sestriere's icy Kandahar piste -- the same one to be used in the world championships.
It was the second year running that Tomba had disappointed his fans, having failed to finish two legs last year.
He then pulled out of a slalom in Chamonix with influenza and missed a giant in the Swiss resort of Adelboden in January, a race with serious implications for Sestriere.
By failing to place in the last giant before the championships, Tomba was pushed out of the group of top 15 seeds in giant slalom for the first time in a decade.

''It is a sign, a signal. It is reality bursting through without taking emotions into account,'' commented La Repubblica newspaper. ''It is time pressing on without pause. It is the frontier between an old story, a glorious and a beautiful one, and a new story about which we know very little and which we want to start well and also have a happy ending.''
There were better portents at the weekend when the Italian finished second in a slalom in Kitzbuehel.

''I could have won this race seeing as how I was only 19 hundredths of a second behind,'' he said. ''And that on a soft piste, the opposite of what is needed to attack. Things will be very different in Sestriere.''
